issues.claim: the first part is probably an old personal name
issues.problem: Sources give more than one theory for the first part (a personal name or an Old English plant name such as comfrey); neither is called 'probable'. Wikipedia also spells the 1275 form Camprichthesheth.
issues.correct: Earliest form Camprichthesheth (1275); the first element may be an unusual personal name or an Old English plant name.
issues.suggested_text: It was recorded in 1275 as Camprichthesheth; the first part may be an old personal name or a plant name. Over time it was changed to look like the familiar 'Cambridge'.

issues.claim: The area stayed rural until a large housing estate was built in the 1950s.
issues.problem: Most of Carpenders Park's houses and bungalows were built in the 1930s (St Meryl Estates); the 1950s added more housing. The big post-war LCC estate (South Oxhey, 1946-52) is on the other side of the line.
issues.correct: Houses and bungalows were mostly built in the 1930s, with further development in the 1950s.
issues.suggested_text: The area stayed rural until houses and bungalows were built in the 1930s. More homes followed in the 1950s.

issues.claim: Probably named after a family called Carpender, who held land here.
issues.problem: No source found that names a Carpender family. Wikipedia, Three Rivers Museum, theundergroundmap and two local-history blogs say only that the area is named after an estate and manor house called Carpenders Park, without explaining that name.
issues.correct: Named after the Carpenders Park estate and its manor house; origin of 'Carpenders' not given in the sources checked.
issues.suggested_head: Named after Carpenders Park, a country estate with a manor house.

issues.claim: It comes from Old English ceaster, a Roman fort or town, and funta, a spring.
issues.problem: The second part is uncertain: Wikipedia gives 'hunt' (hunting ground or huntsman) as one reading and funta (spring) as an alternative. The head hedges, but the text states funta as fact.
issues.correct: First part ceaster (Roman fort) is secure; second part may be funta (spring) or hunt (hunting ground).
issues.suggested_text: It probably comes from Old English ceaster, a Roman fort or town, and funta, a spring. The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Cestrehunt.

issues.problem: Wikipedia says the meaning is not certain and calls the 'shingly ford' theory 'likely to be incorrect' (the word shingle for river stones is not found before the 1500s). Other ideas: a ford on the River Ching, or 'ford of the dwellers by the stumps' on the Lea. So 'probably' and 'over a stony bed' are not supported.
issues.correct: Recorded as Cingeford (913) and Cingefort (Domesday 1086); meaning uncertain; ford may have been on the Ching or the Lea. Hunting Lodge: commissioned by Henry VIII 1542, completed 1543 (correct).
issues.suggested_head: Chingford is named after an old ford, but nobody is sure what 'Ching' means.
issues.suggested_text: The idea of a 'shingle ford' is now doubted; the ford may have crossed the River Ching or the Lea. On the edge of Epping Forest stands Queen Elizabeth's Hunting Lodge, built for Henry VIII in 1543.

issues.claim: The station was called Chorley Wood, in two words, until 1964.
issues.problem: Wrong year. The name changed to Chorleywood in 1965 (it was Chorley Wood 1889-1915 and 1934-1965, Chorley Wood & Chenies 1915-1934).
issues.suggested_text: Ceorl is the Old English word that gave us 'churl'. The 'wood' part needs no explanation. The station was called Chorley Wood, in two words, until 1965.

issues.claim: The station opened in 1902 as Dagenham and became Dagenham East in 1949.
issues.problem: The station opened in 1885 (London, Tilbury and Southend Railway). 1902 is when District line trains started serving it.
issues.correct: Opened 1 May 1885 as Dagenham by the LT&SR; District services from 2 June 1902; renamed Dagenham East 1949.
issues.suggested_text: It was first written down in 666 as Dæccanhaam, in a charter of Barking Abbey. The station opened in 1885 as Dagenham, District trains came in 1902, and it became Dagenham East in 1949.

issues.claim: It was recorded in 1395 as Kyngeslond, probably royal land used for hunting.
issues.problem: Could not confirm the 1395 / Kyngeslond record online (Wikipedia, Hidden London and British History Online do not give it). Hidden London says only that the name comes from royal ownership of parts of Hackney; Wikipedia links it to hunting grounds of a Tudor royal house at Newington Green, which would be later than 1395, so the hunting explanation does not fit the date well.
issues.correct: Name reflects former royal ownership of land in Hackney (Hidden London); hunting link only in Wikipedia and tied to the Tudor period.
issues.suggested_text: It was recorded in 1395 as Kyngeslond, land owned by the king. Dalston means the farm of a man called Deorlaf.

issues.claim: The valley is that of the River Roding.
issues.problem: Wikipedia gives the meaning (Old English dep + denu, deep valley) but does not say which valley. British History Online (Loughton) places the old manor of Debden (Debden Hall and Green) at the north of the estate and mentions the Roding only as the parish boundary. Could not confirm the Roding link.
issues.correct: 'Deep valley' is supported; which valley is not stated in sources checked.
issues.suggested_text: The name comes from an old manor nearby. The station opened in 1865 on a railway line and was called Chigwell Lane until 1949, when the Central line took it over.

issues.problem: Wrong borough. The station is in the Royal Borough of Greenwich, close to the Lewisham boundary.
